summary: A status report saying the UCSB remote job entry and output retrieval services described in RFC 105 had been used successfully from Rand. Rand users reached them through a network service program on video-graphic consoles, and one Rand research group had started using the facility for real work. It is an early report of a working ARPANET service.

plainLanguage.summary: Rand sent piles of punched cards to a computer at UCSB over the network and got the printed results back. This report says it worked, lists how fast it went, and notes a few messages that were lost or scrambled.

questions: did the ucsb remote job entry service work from rand
what was the network service program at rand
how fast was early arpanet file transfer
subtitle: A 1971 field report on using UCSB's remote job service from Rand, with timings and a few failures.

tldr.problem: Early network users needed to know whether sending work to a remote computer actually succeeded in practice.
tldr.mechanism: Rand reports on running jobs at UCSB through its Network Service Program, giving typical job sizes, a timing study, and a list of failures it observed.
tldr.outcome: The service worked and was used for real work on a limited basis, but transfer was slow at about 250 cards per minute, and a few messages failed for reasons that were never found.

today: RFC 113 is a 1971 status report rather than a specification, and the unit metadata lists RFC 227 as a later update.

sections.title: Using UCSB's Remote Job Service From Rand
sections.content:
The UCSB Remote Job Entry (RJE) and Remote Job Output Retrieval (RJOR) systems, described in RFC 105, were used and validated from Rand. The facility was then in limited production use by another research group at Rand.

Rand reached UCSB through its Network Service Program (NSP), driven by Rand Video-Graphic consoles. That program gives a console user access to both local file storage at Rand and to the network. A small module, UCSBMGR, was added to NSP to handle the UCSB RJE and RJOR protocols and data formats.

Typical jobs were input decks of 800 to 2800 80-character card images, with output files of about 30 pages of printer listings.
sections.plainLanguage: Rand's computer learned to send a stack of work to a computer at UCSB and receive the printed answers. The report describes how the connection was set up and how large a typical job was.

sections.title: Speed of Transfer
sections.content:
A timing study of a 2800-record file gave an average rate of 250 80-character cards per minute, with each card sent as a separate network message. The authors note this is much less than the advertised 30 kilobit rate, though the path from Rand to UCSB passes through at least one intermediate IMP.

The processes at each end ran at maximum priority and with very small loads on either machine, so slow machines were not the cause. The authors suggest that blocking card images together for network transmission would be an obvious way to speed things up.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending each card in its own message was slow, a bit like mailing every page of a book in a separate envelope. Putting several cards into one message would speed it up.

sections.title: Failures Observed
sections.content:
Over about two months of networking, the authors saw approximately five serious failures in transmitted messages. In two cases the RFNM on the control link from UCSB to Rand was lost, and the loss was not reported by a type 9 IMP-to-Host message as would be expected. They could not make the problem happen again, so they could not tell whether the IMP or the UCSB host interface was at fault.

The other three failures were garbled data messages, and each time it was the second card image sent to RJE. The HASP system at UCSB ignored the image instead of printing it, so the cause stayed unknown. The problem appeared sporadically in early transmissions and then disappeared. The authors were fairly confident their host software at either end was not at fault, and they note that over 100 jobs had been run at UCSB from Rand, each with many network transmissions.
sections.plainLanguage: A few times a message was lost or scrambled and no one could find out why. Since then the problem stopped, and more than a hundred jobs ran without trouble.

references.text: NWG/RFC #105, describing the UCSB RJE and RJOR systems.
